readings.title: A shared ride to the market
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
Residents in a small village shared rides to a weekly market. Several drivers arrived with empty seats while others were asked too late. The main obstacle was requests scattered across private messages. No coordinator could see who needed a ride or what time they planned to return. At first, the people involved did not agree on which part of the proposal deserved the most attention.

To investigate, the team used a simple booking record for two market days. Volunteers recorded preferred times and checked accessibility needs without sharing personal details publicly. The organizers kept the first stage small enough to change without wasting substantial time or resources.

The evidence indicated one contact point reduced missed journeys. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a weekly request deadline and backup contact. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. The records were useful because they described ordinary use rather than an ideal situation imagined at a meeting.

The case suggests a broader point: shared travel depends on clear coordination. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The group published its reasons so that people who preferred a different result could still understand the choice. For those taking part in a shared ride to the market, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records.

readings.title: Reaching an evening class by bus
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
An adult college opened an evening course in a rural town. Learners could reach the first lesson by bus but could not get home afterward. The main obstacle was a timetable planned around the outward journey. The last return bus departed shortly before the class finished. The question mattered to people with different schedules and levels of experience, so one account could not represent everyone.

To investigate, the team used a comparison of class and bus times. The college asked learners where they travelled from and discussed feasible options with transport staff. A simple record of what happened each day gave the team a starting point for comparison.

The evidence indicated a small class-time shift helped several villages. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a revised start time and published return guidance. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Some participants welcomed the change immediately, while others noticed practical details that needed further work.

The case suggests a broader point: access requires planning the whole trip. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The result was a revised plan, not a claim that every difficulty had disappeared. For those taking part in reaching an evening class by bus, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: A mobile library stop
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A mobile library visited four villages. Its stop in one village was beside a steep road, making it difficult for some readers to board. The main obstacle was a stop chosen for parking convenience alone. The vehicle had space, but the path from nearby homes was uneven. The initial idea sounded reasonable, yet the details of the place made it harder to carry out than expected.

To investigate, the team used a route assessment with regular users. Staff compared safe parking places and asked readers where they approached from. Instead of relying on a single opinion, the team invited several users to describe what they actually did.

The evidence indicated a level site nearby was more accessible. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a relocated stop with advance notice. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. This allowed the organizers to separate a temporary inconvenience from a pattern that required attention.

The case suggests a broader point: a useful service must be reachable on foot. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. They also decided when to check the arrangement again, because conditions could change over time. For those taking part in a mobile library stop, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Delivering medicine to remote homes
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A rural pharmacy arranged medicine deliveries for people who could not travel easily. Drivers sometimes arrived when recipients were at appointments. The main obstacle was delivery windows that were too broad. People knew the day but not whether the driver would come morning or afternoon. The people affected were invited to comment before a permanent arrangement was chosen.

To investigate, the team used a review of failed delivery attempts. The pharmacy grouped routes and asked customers how they preferred to confirm availability. The first trial produced both useful results and questions the team could not yet answer.

The evidence indicated shorter windows reduced wasted journeys. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a telephone confirmation before the route. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Rather than hide those limits, the public note explained how the next version had been selected.

The case suggests a broader point: reliable delivery balances efficiency and personal needs. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. That explanation made later changes easier to discuss with residents and staff. For those taking part in delivering medicine to remote homes, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

translation.stem:
Translate the following passage into Chinese:
Projects concerning rural travel and service access often begin with a practical question. People may agree on a general goal while experiencing the same service in different ways. In this case, local organizers invited residents to describe ordinary visits and kept simple records of what happened. They compared those accounts before changing the rural access coordination programme. The first trial did not answer every question, but it showed which difficulties were repeated and which were temporary. Staff then explained the reasons for a modest adjustment. Clear information helped people understand the decision, including those who would have preferred another option. The group planned to review the arrangement again after more people had used it.
translation.explanation: 参考译文供考生自评，注意语义准确、逻辑关系及汉语通顺。
translation.referenceAnswer: 有关乡村出行与服务衔接的项目通常从一个实际问题开始。人们可能赞同总体目标，却对同一服务有不同体验。在这个案例中，当地组织者请居民描述日常使用情况，并简单记录发生的事情。他们对照这些叙述后调整了服务。最初的试行无法回答所有问题，但能显示哪些困难反复出现，哪些只是暂时现象。工作人员随后解释了一项适度调整的原因。清楚的信息帮助人们理解决定，包括那些更希望采用其他方案的人。团队计划在更多人使用后再次评估安排。

writing.stem: Write at least 100 words in English to the rural transport team proposing a small improvement to the rural access coordination programme. Explain the problem, describe a short trial, and say what evidence should guide the final decision.
writing.explanation: 范文供考生自评，注意任务要点、组织结构及语言准确性。
writing.sampleAnswer:
Dear Committee Members,
I would like to propose a small improvement to the rural access coordination programme. People have noticed requests scattered across private messages, and a short trial could help us understand how often this problem occurs. We should ask regular users and people who have not used the service before to describe their experiences. Their comments may reveal details that a plan made in an office would miss.
For one month, staff could keep a simple record of participation, time spent and any difficulties reported. We should also explain the purpose of the trial in clear language so that residents know how to contribute. After the month, please publish a brief summary of both benefits and limits. The final decision should be based on what people actually experienced, with a date for checking the arrangement again.
Yours sincerely,
A resident
